reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: An evacuatory disorder characterised by straining, incomplete evacuation, a sense of anorectal blockage, prolonged toileting, and the need for manual manoeuvres such as vaginal or perineal splinting or digitation

Broadly divided into mechanical causes (rectocele, internal rectal intussusception, enterocele, sigmoidocele) and functional causes (dyssynergic defecation or anismus, poor propulsion, rectal hyposensitivity)
More common in women, in whom an anterior rectocele frequently traps stool
Assessment combines symptom scoring, careful rectal and vaginal examination, defecography, and anorectal physiology to define the mechanism
Initial management is conservative: fibre and fluid, laxatives, toileting and behavioural advice, and pelvic floor biofeedback, especially where dyssynergia coexists
Surgery (for example stapled transanal rectal resection, rectocele repair, or ventral rectopexy) is reserved for significant structural lesions after conservative measures fail
Frequently coexists with mucosal prolapse, solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and pelvic organ prolapse
reference.pathophysiology: Obstructed defecation results from failure to evacuate the rectum despite the urge, due to mechanical outlet obstruction, functional pelvic floor dysfunction, or both. Mechanical contributors include an anterior rectocele that traps stool, internal rectal intussusception, enterocele, and sigmoidocele; functional contributors include paradoxical puborectalis contraction (anismus), impaired rectal propulsion, and reduced rectal sensation. Chronic straining aggravates prolapse and perineal descent, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. The disorder overlaps with mucosal prolapse syndromes and pelvic organ prolapse.
additionalDifferentials: Internal rectal intussusception or full-thickness prolapse
additionalInvestigations: Defecography (fluoroscopic or MR) to demonstrate rectocele, intussusception, enterocele, and evacuation
Anorectal manometry to assess pressures and identify dyssynergia
Balloon expulsion test as a functional screen for evacuatory dysfunction
Colonic transit studies to distinguish slow transit from outlet obstruction
Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude mucosal disease and malignancy
Endoanal ultrasound where sphincter integrity is relevant
redFlags: New-onset constipation with bleeding, weight loss, or anaemia suggesting malignancy
A palpable rectal or pelvic mass
Progressive symptoms with obstructive features suggesting a stricture
Faecal incontinence or neurological signs suggesting a neurogenic cause
reference.prognosis: Symptoms often improve with conservative measures and biofeedback where dyssynergia predominates; results of surgery for structural lesions are variable, and recurrence or persistent symptoms are common, so careful patient selection matters.
pitfalls: Operating on an incidental rectocele that is not the true cause of symptoms
Overlooking coexisting dyssynergia treatable by biofeedback before surgery
Failing to distinguish outlet obstruction from slow-transit constipation
Missing an obstructing neoplasm in new-onset symptoms
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
management: First-line conservative management with increased dietary fibre and fluid, laxatives, and toileting and behavioural advice
Pelvic floor biofeedback and retraining, particularly where dyssynergic defecation (anismus) coexists
Manual and positional evacuation strategies, including vaginal or perineal splinting
Surgery reserved for significant structural lesions after conservative measures fail, such as stapled transanal rectal resection, rectocele repair or ventral rectopexy
Exclusion of mucosal disease and malignancy before attributing symptoms to a functional or structural evacuatory disorder
Multidisciplinary pelvic floor assessment integrating colorectal surgery, gynaecology and specialist physiotherapy for careful patient selection
